subject: chem
title: Analytical Techniques
subtitle: Mass spectrometry, IR spectroscopy, NMR and chromatography.
concept: Mass spectrometry identifies molecular mass and fragments; IR spectroscopy identifies functional groups from characteristic absorption frequencies.
¹H NMR reveals the environment of hydrogen atoms, enabling structural determination from chemical shift, splitting pattern and integration.
Chromatography separates mixtures; Rf values and retention times identify compounds.

notes.heading: Mass Spectrometry (Revisited)
items: High-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) measures the exact molecular mass to several decimal places, allowing identification of the molecular formula. Different formulae with the same nominal mass (e.g. CO vs N₂ vs CH₂=CH₂) can be distinguished.

Fragmentation patterns are characteristic of functional groups: loss of 15 (CH₃), 29 (CHO or C₂H₅), 31 (OCH₃), 45 (OC₂H₅ or COOH) etc. The M−1 peak often arises from loss of H; M+1 and M+2 patterns reveal the presence of Cl or Br isotopes.

notes.heading: Infrared Spectroscopy
items: IR spectroscopy identifies functional groups from characteristic absorption wavenumbers (cm⁻¹). Key absorptions: O–H (alcohol) broad 3200–3550; O–H (carboxylic acid) very broad 2500–3300; N–H (amine) 3300–3500 (one or two peaks); C=O (carbonyl) strong sharp 1680–1750 (position distinguishes type: acid ~1710, ester ~1735–1750, ketone ~1715, amide ~1630–1680); C–H 2850–3100; C≡N nitrile ~2200.
The fingerprint region (below ~1500 cm⁻¹) contains a complex, unique pattern for each compound — used to confirm identity by comparison with a reference spectrum.

notes.heading: ¹H NMR Spectroscopy
items: ¹H NMR identifies the chemical environments of hydrogen atoms. Chemical shift δ (ppm) is measured relative to TMS (δ = 0) — the chosen reference because all 12 protons are equivalent, it is chemically inert, and it is volatile.
Typical shifts: R–CH₃ ~0.9; R–CH₂–R ~1.2–1.4; R–CO–CH₃ ~2.1; Ar–H ~7–8; R–CHO ~9–10; R–COOH ~10–12.

Integration: the area under each peak is proportional to the number of H atoms in that environment. Splitting (n+1 rule): a proton with n equivalent neighbouring H atoms gives a peak split into n+1 lines. Classic ethyl group: –CH₂– (quartet, 3 neighbours) and –CH₃ (triplet, 2 neighbours).
D₂O shake: exchangeable protons (–OH, –NH) are replaced by deuterium — the corresponding NMR peak disappears, confirming –OH or –NH groups.

notes.heading: Chromatography
items: In all forms of chromatography, components separate by their different affinities for the mobile phase (which moves) versus the stationary phase (which does not). Rf = distance moved by component / distance moved by solvent front (TLC/paper).

Gas-liquid chromatography (GLC): volatile compounds separate in a column; each component gives a peak at a characteristic retention time. GC–MS combines separation with mass spectrometry — the most powerful technique for identifying unknown mixture components.

definitions.body: The position of an NMR peak in parts per million (ppm) relative to TMS; reflects the electronic environment of the hydrogen atom.
The IR region below ~1500 cm⁻¹ containing a complex pattern of absorptions unique to each compound.
In ¹H NMR, a proton with n equivalent neighbouring H atoms appears as a split peak with n+1 lines (doublet, triplet, quartet etc.).

workedExamples.q: An IR spectrum shows a strong absorption at ~1715 cm⁻¹ and a broad absorption at 2500–3300 cm⁻¹. Identify the functional groups.

steps.text: Strong, sharp absorption at ~1715 cm⁻¹ indicates a C=O stretch; 1715 is typical for a carboxylic acid.
Broad absorption at 2500–3300 cm⁻¹ is characteristic of O–H stretch in a carboxylic acid.
Compound contains a carboxylic acid (–COOH) group.

mistakes: Confusing the broad O–H absorption of a carboxylic acid (2500–3300) with an alcohol O–H (3200–3550 cm⁻¹); carboxylic acid O–H is broader and extends to lower wavenumber.
Applying n+1 rule incorrectly: count only equivalent H atoms on adjacent carbons.
Forgetting that integration gives ratio of H atoms, not actual numbers.
tips: IR: 'sharp and strong at ~1700–1750' = always a C=O; determine which type from position and other peaks.
NMR: a quartet (4 lines) means 3 adjacent H; a triplet (3 lines) means 2 adjacent H — classic ethyl group: quartet + triplet.
TMS is the NMR reference: inert, volatile, all 12 H equivalent → single sharp peak at δ 0.

flashcards.q: What does the molecular ion peak in mass spectrometry tell you?
flashcards.a: The relative molecular mass (Mr) of the compound.

flashcards.q: What IR absorption indicates a carboxylic acid?
flashcards.a: Broad O–H absorption at 2500–3300 cm⁻¹ AND strong C=O absorption at ~1700–1725 cm⁻¹.

flashcards.q: In ¹H NMR, what does a quartet (4 lines) indicate about neighbouring protons?
flashcards.a: 3 equivalent neighbouring H atoms (n+1 rule: 3+1 = 4 lines).

flashcards.q: What is TMS and why is it used as an NMR reference?
flashcards.a: Tetramethylsilane Si(CH₃)₄: gives a single sharp peak at δ 0 (assigned); all 12H equivalent; chemically inert; volatile (easily removed).

flashcards.q: How does D₂O shake help in ¹H NMR?
flashcards.a: Exchangeable protons (–OH, –NH) are replaced by D → the corresponding NMR peak disappears → confirms the presence of –OH or –NH.

flashcards.q: What does a high m/z fragment at (M – 15) in a mass spectrum suggest?
flashcards.a: Loss of CH₃ (mass 15) from the molecular ion — suggests a methyl group in the compound.

questions.q: A compound shows a strong IR absorption at ~1735 cm⁻¹ but no broad O–H absorption. What functional group is present?
questions.exp: Ester C=O absorbs at ~1735–1750 cm⁻¹; no O–H stretch — consistent with ester (RCOOR').

questions.q: In ¹H NMR, the integration ratio of peaks is 3:2:1. What does this tell you?
questions.exp: Integration gives the ratio of the number of H atoms in each environment — here, 3 H : 2 H : 1 H environments.

questions.q: In a mass spectrum, what does the M+2 peak (roughly 1/3 intensity of M peak) suggest?
questions.exp: Chlorine has two isotopes ³⁵Cl (75%) and ³⁷Cl (25%), giving M and M+2 peaks in ratio ~3:1.

questions.q: A ¹H NMR peak appears at δ ~9.5–10 ppm. What functional group does this suggest?
questions.exp: Aldehyde proton (–CHO) resonates at δ ~9–10 ppm due to deshielding by the adjacent C=O.

questions.q: What is Rf in chromatography?
opts: Retention factor = distance of solvent / distance of spot
Distance of spot / distance of solvent front
Rate of flow of mobile phase
questions.exp: Rf = distance moved by compound spot / distance moved by solvent front. Values between 0 and 1.

questions.q: In a mass spectrum, which peak gives the relative molecular mass?
questions.exp: The molecular ion peak M⁺ at the highest m/z value corresponds to the intact molecule losing one electron — it gives Mᵣ directly.

questions.q: What does the base peak in a mass spectrum represent?
questions.exp: The base peak is the tallest peak in the spectrum — the most abundant (most stable) fragment ion. It is assigned a relative abundance of 100%.

questions.q: Which IR absorption at ~1710 cm⁻¹ is characteristic of?
questions.exp: A strong, sharp absorption at 1680–1750 cm⁻¹ is the C=O stretch. The exact position identifies the carbonyl type: acid ~1710, ester ~1735, ketone ~1715.

questions.q: In ¹H NMR, a signal split into a quartet has how many neighbouring H atoms?
questions.exp: By the n+1 rule: a signal split into (n+1) lines means n equivalent neighbouring H atoms. A quartet = 4 lines, so n = 3 neighbouring H atoms.

questions.q: What does the D₂O shake test in NMR confirm?
questions.exp: D₂O replaces exchangeable protons (–OH, –NH, –COOH) with deuterium; the corresponding NMR signal disappears, confirming these functional groups.

questions.q: A compound shows M⁺ at m/z 58 and a fragment at m/z 43 (loss of 15). What fragment was lost?
questions.exp: Loss of 15 mass units corresponds to loss of a CH₃ group (Ar = 12+3×1 = 15). This is a very common fragmentation in ketones and branched alkanes.

questions.q: Which technique is most powerful for identifying components in a complex mixture?
questions.exp: GC–MS combines separation (by GC) with identification (by MS) — each component gives a retention time AND a unique mass spectrum, making it the gold standard for mixture analysis.

questions.q: In the ¹H NMR of ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH), how many distinct signals are observed?
questions.exp: Ethanol has 3 distinct hydrogen environments: –CH₃ (3H, triplet), –CH₂– (2H, quartet), and –OH (1H, singlet or broad). Total: 3 signals.

questions.q: A compound with formula C₄H₈O shows an IR absorption at 1715 cm⁻¹ and no O–H peak. What is it most likely?
questions.exp: C=O at 1715 cm⁻¹ (ketone range) with no broad O–H absorption rules out acid or alcohol. C₄H₈O with a ketone is butanone (methyl ethyl ketone).

questions.q: Which statement about the fingerprint region (< 1500 cm⁻¹) of an IR spectrum is correct?
opts: It contains only O–H and N–H stretches
It is unique to each compound and used for identification by comparison
It always shows a C=O peak
It is too complex to interpret and is ignored
questions.exp: The fingerprint region is complex and unique — like a fingerprint for the molecule. It is used to confirm identity by comparing against a reference spectrum of the known compound.

questions.q: Which technique gives the molecular ion peak M⁺?
questions.exp: The mass spectrum gives the M⁺ peak at the highest m/z, corresponding to the relative molecular mass.

questions.q: In ¹H NMR, what does TMS (tetramethylsilane) provide?
questions.exp: TMS provides 12 equivalent protons at δ = 0 ppm, used as the zero reference for chemical shift.

questions.q: A compound shows a broad IR absorption at 2500–3300 cm⁻¹. What functional group is present?
questions.exp: Carboxylic acids show a very broad O–H stretch at 2500–3300 cm⁻¹ due to strong hydrogen bonding.

questions.q: The n+1 rule in ¹H NMR predicts splitting. A CH₂ group adjacent to a CH₃ group appears as a:
questions.exp: The CH₂ has 2 neighbours on the CH₃, so n+1 = 2+1 = 3 lines (triplet).

questions.q: In GLC (gas-liquid chromatography), what does the retention time indicate?
opts: The molecular mass of the compound
The identity of the compound by comparison
questions.exp: Each compound has a characteristic retention time under fixed conditions; comparison with standards identifies it.

questions.q: A mass spectrum shows equal M and M+2 peaks. Which halogen is present?
questions.exp: Bromine has two isotopes (⁷⁹Br : ⁸¹Br ≈ 1:1), giving equal M and M+2 peaks. Chlorine gives M : M+2 ≈ 3:1.

questions.q: An unknown compound has δ ~10 ppm in ¹H NMR and a strong C=O at ~1710 cm⁻¹ in IR. What is it?
questions.exp: δ 10–12 ppm = COOH proton; ~1710 cm⁻¹ C=O stretch is consistent with carboxylic acid.

questions.q: The fingerprint region in IR spectroscopy is below which wavenumber?
questions.exp: Below ~1500 cm⁻¹ is the fingerprint region — a unique pattern for each compound used for identity confirmation.

questions.q: Integration of ¹H NMR peaks tells you:
opts: Number of H atoms in each environment
questions.exp: The area under each NMR peak is proportional to the number of protons in that chemical environment.

questions.q: In a mass spectrum, the base peak is:
questions.exp: The base peak is the tallest peak in the mass spectrum — the most stable fragment produced.

recall: Describe how a mass spectrum gives the molecular mass of a compound.
Identify functional groups from IR absorption positions.
Interpret a ¹H NMR spectrum (chemical shift, integration, splitting).
Explain the n+1 rule with an example.
Calculate Rf and explain its use in identifying compounds.
